title: Passage planning and heavy weather
summary: Building a weather picture, choosing a window, ports of refuge, and heavy-weather preparation and tactics.

segments.heading: Building the picture
paragraphs: Start several days out: follow the synoptic and forecast charts to understand the pattern and how it is evolving. Closer to departure, add the official marine forecast, inshore forecasts, gale warnings and GRIB data from more than one model. Note where forecasts disagree; disagreement is a measure of uncertainty.

Then apply it to your boat and crew. What is the strongest likely wind including gusts, from which direction relative to your course and the tidal streams, for how long, and with what sea state at headlands and in the approach to your destination?
keyPoints: Follow the pattern for days, not just the latest forecast.
Model disagreement means uncertainty: add margin.
Translate wind and sea into conditions on your route.

segments.heading: Limits, timing and refuges
paragraphs: Set personal limits for wind, sea and visibility before you read the forecast, and agree them with the crew. Time departure so that the passage ends in daylight and the worst of any front or wind shift is met in open water, not at a lee-shore harbour entrance.

List ports of refuge along the route, noting which are safe to enter in the forecast wind direction, at what states of tide, and in darkness. Remember that a forecast veer can turn a refuge into a dangerous entrance.

segments.heading: Set your limits before you look
paragraphs: Decide your limits before reading the forecast, so the forecast cannot talk you into going. For this boat and crew: the strongest wind including gusts, the highest sea state, wind direction relative to the course, minimum visibility, and whether you will arrive in daylight. Lower the limits for a tired, inexperienced or small crew.

Then check the forecast against those limits for the whole passage plus a margin, not just the departure time. Identify fallback ports you can reach in the forecast wind, and the point beyond which turning back is no longer the safer option.
keyPoints: Fix limits first: wind and gusts, sea, direction, visibility, daylight.
Check the whole passage plus a margin.
Name fallback ports and the point of no return.

segments.heading: Triggers, and motor versus sail
paragraphs: Agree triggers for changing the plan before you leave: a new warning, the barometer falling faster than forecast, the wind or sea above your limits, slower progress than planned, or a tiring crew. When a trigger is met, act on it; do not wait for the next forecast.

Boat type changes the decision. A motor cruiser can use speed to fit a short window, but must slow right down in head seas, depends on fuel and on the engine, and can broach in steep following seas. A sailing yacht is slower, so stays exposed for longer, but can keep moving without the engine. Base the plan on realistic speed in the expected sea, not on flat-water speed.
keyPoints: Agree triggers in advance and act when one is met.
Plan on realistic speed in the expected sea.
Motor: speed, fuel, head and following seas. Sail: longer exposure.

segments.heading: Before it arrives
paragraphs: Reef early. Stow and secure everything below and on deck, close hatches and seacocks not in use, rig jackstays and ensure everyone wears lifejackets and harnesses on deck. Prepare hot food and drinks and simple snacks, set a watch rota that protects the crew from fatigue, and brief everyone on the plan and on seasickness management.
Fix your position and plan sea room: the greatest danger in heavy weather is usually the land, not the sea.
keyPoints: Reef early and secure the boat.
Feed and rest the crew; keep sea room.

segments.heading: Tactics
paragraphs: Options include continuing under deeply reefed sail, heaving-to (backed headsail, eased main, helm lashed to windward) to rest the crew and ride the seas comfortably, running off under minimal sail with warps or a drogue to control speed, and in survival conditions a sea anchor from the bow.

There is no universal tactic. The right choice depends on sail or power, hull form and stability, the size, shape and period of the seas, sea room, visibility, the crew and the builder's guidance. Better still, avoid it: divert or seek shelter early, reduce speed and reassess often, and decide while the crew still has energy.

questions.prompt: Three models disagree by 12 hours on when a front will arrive. What does this tell you?
options: Use the most optimistic model
Forecast uncertainty is high; build in a margin or wait
Average them and leave on the average
Ignore models and use the barometer only
optionExplanations: Picking the best case is wishful thinking.
Correct.
An average hides the spread.
The barometer complements, not replaces, forecasts.
questions.explanation: Disagreement between models quantifies uncertainty. Plan for the earlier arrival or delay.

questions.prompt: When should you set your personal wind limits for a passage?
options: After reading the forecast
Before reading the forecast
Once at sea
Only if a gale is forecast
optionExplanations: That invites talking yourself into it.
Correct.
Too late.
Limits apply to all conditions.
questions.explanation: Fixed limits set in advance protect against optimistic reading of a marginal forecast.

questions.prompt: A gale is forecast in 8 hours and you are committed to the passage. Which preparations should you make now? Select all that apply.
options: Reef before the wind rises
Prepare hot food and flasks
Open hatches for ventilation
Rig jackstays and wear harnesses
Plan to stay well offshore away from a lee shore
optionExplanations: Correct.
Correct.
Hatches must be closed and secured.
Correct.
Correct: sea room is safety.
questions.explanation: Prepare the boat, the crew and the plan before conditions deteriorate.

options: Running downwind under bare poles
Backed headsail, eased mainsail and helm lashed to windward so the boat lies quietly
Motoring into the wind at full power
Anchoring in deep water
optionExplanations: That is running off.
Correct.
Not heaving-to.
Not heaving-to.
questions.explanation: Heaving-to stops the boat in a comfortable attitude, giving the crew a rest and time to deal with problems.

questions.context: You plan a 60-mile passage along a south-facing coast. Forecast: 'West 4 to 5, increasing 6 to 7 later, veering north-west.' Your planned destination harbour has a bar entrance facing west, dangerous in strong westerlies and on the ebb. An alternative harbour, 40 miles along, faces south-east with an all-tide entrance.
questions.explanation: Avoid the exposed west-facing bar in a rising westerly; the south-east-facing harbour is sheltered from the forecast west to north-west wind.

steps.prompt: Why is the planned destination a poor choice?
options: The bar faces the rising westerly and may break on the ebb
It is too far
It has no fuel
Harbours are always dangerous at night
optionExplanations: Correct.
Distance is not the main issue.
Irrelevant to safety here.
Too general.
steps.explanation: A west-facing bar with a strong westerly and an ebb running out can break dangerously.

steps.prompt: Will the south-east-facing harbour stay sheltered after the veer to north-west?
options: Yes: its entrance faces away from both westerly and north-westerly winds
No: the veer makes it a lee shore
Only at high water
Only in daylight
optionExplanations: Correct.
A north-westerly blows offshore at a south-east-facing entrance.
It is an all-tide entrance.
Not the deciding factor.
steps.explanation: An entrance facing south-east is in the lee of both west and north-west winds.

options: Plan for the alternative harbour as the destination from the start
Head for the bar and decide on arrival
Delay until the gale is blowing to check its strength
Anchor off the bar
optionExplanations: Correct: shorter, sheltered, all-tide.
Deciding at a breaking bar is too late.
Waiting into the gale reduces options.
An open anchorage off a lee bar is dangerous.
steps.explanation: Choose the destination that stays safe in the forecast's worst stage.

questions.prompt: In heavy weather offshore, what is usually the greatest danger?
options: The waves themselves
The land: a lee shore and loss of sea room
Running out of food
Cold
optionExplanations: Waves are a risk, but well-found boats cope with sea room.
Correct.
Manageable with preparation.
Manageable with clothing.
questions.explanation: Sea room is safety. Most heavy-weather losses involve the land.

questions.prompt: Running off before large breaking seas, the boat is surfing dangerously fast. What helps?
options: Hoisting more sail
Streaming warps or a drogue to slow her
Steering exactly square to every crest at full speed
Turning beam-on to the seas
optionExplanations: More sail increases speed.
Correct.
Excess speed risks pitchpoling or broaching.
Beam-on risks a knockdown.
questions.explanation: Controlling speed with drag devices reduces the risk of broaching or pitchpoling.

questions.prompt: Conditions are worse than forecast and the crew is tiring. What is the seamanlike response?
options: Press on to the plan
Reassess: divert, heave-to or turn back as needed
Increase sail to arrive sooner
Wait for the next forecast before doing anything
optionExplanations: The plan was based on a forecast that is now wrong.
Correct.
More sail adds risk.
Act on what you see now.
questions.explanation: Changing plan in response to conditions is good seamanship.

questions.context: In May you plan to sail west from Weymouth to Dartmouth, about 50 miles, rounding Portland Bill. Boat: 10 m yacht, crew of three. Your limits: Force 6, moderate sea, arrive in daylight. Forecast issued 05:00: 'West or south-west 4 or 5, occasionally 6 later. Moderate. Fair. Good.' Off the Bill the stream runs west from 10:00 to 16:00 and east from 16:00 to 22:00.
questions.explanation: Time the race, keep well clear of it, set triggers, and turn back to shelter when a warning makes the rest of the passage a beat into a rising gale in the dark.

steps.prompt: How do you deal with Portland Race?
options: Go through the middle of the race at maximum westgoing stream
Keep well clear, or use the inshore passage at the time the pilot book gives
Go through at 16:00 whatever the wind
Ignore it: Force 4 to 5 is moderate
optionExplanations: Wind against a strong stream in the race: steep breaking seas.
Correct: follow the pilot book's timing and clearances.
Timing must suit both stream and wind.
Races can be dangerous in moderate winds.
steps.explanation: Keep well off a race or use the recognised inshore passage at the right time.

steps.prompt: At 11:00, abeam the Bill, a gale warning is broadcast: 'Westerly gale 8 expected later'. When is the gale expected?
options: Within 6 hours
6 to 12 hours
More than 12 hours after issue
It is already blowing
optionExplanations: That is 'imminent'.
That is 'soon'.
Correct: 'later' means more than 12 hours after issue.
Not yet.
steps.explanation: 'Later' is more than 12 hours from the time of issue.

steps.prompt: Dartmouth is 42 miles on. Beating into the westerly your speed made good is 4 knots. How many hours to arrive?
steps.explanation: 42 ÷ 4 is 10½ hours: arriving around 21:30, after dark, as the wind rises.

options: Press on: the gale is not due for 12 hours
Turn back to Weymouth, downwind and sheltered from the west
Heave to off the Bill and wait
Motor into it at full power to save time
optionExplanations: You would beat into rising wind and arrive in the dark, beyond your limits.
Correct: a short, downwind run to a harbour sheltered from westerlies.
Close to the race and a lee shore in a rising westerly.
Head seas will slow you and tire the crew.
steps.explanation: Your daylight and wind limits will both be broken; the fallback port is close and downwind.

questions.context: July, in the Cyclades. You plan to sail from Kythnos east to Syros, about 25 miles. The national forecast: 'North 5 to 6 Beaufort, locally 7 in the central Aegean from midday; similar for the next three days.' Your crew of four includes two beginners.
questions.explanation: The Meltemi usually builds through the day and is strongest in the channels and off capes. Leave early, expect funnelling and lee gusts, and choose shelter from the north.

options: At first light, before the wind builds
Mid-afternoon, when it is warmest
At midday, when the forecast says 7
At dusk, when it always drops
optionExplanations: Correct: the Meltemi is usually lightest in the early morning.
Usually the windiest part of the day.
The forecast's strongest period.
It often eases at night, but arriving at an unfamiliar island in the dark adds risk.
steps.explanation: Leave early to complete the passage before the afternoon peak.

steps.prompt: Where on the route do you expect the strongest wind?
options: In the lee of Kythnos at departure
In the open channel between the islands and off the capes
In Syros harbour
It is uniform
optionExplanations: The lee is gusty but less wind overall.
Correct: funnelling between islands and acceleration off capes.
Harbours are usually sheltered.
Islands make it very uneven.
steps.explanation: Expect a force or more extra in the channels and off headlands.

steps.prompt: Which anchorage gives the best shelter for the night?
options: A bay open to the north
A bay on the south side, open to the south
An open roadstead on the east coast
Any bay, since the wind drops at night
optionExplanations: Open to the Meltemi and its sea.
Correct: but expect gusts down the slopes in the lee of high ground.
Exposed to swell wrapping round.
It may not drop, and can blow all night.
steps.explanation: Choose shelter from the north, and allow for downslope gusts.

steps.prompt: On day two the forecast becomes 'North 7, locally 8'. With two beginners aboard, what do you do?
options: Sail as planned
Stay in harbour and wait for the Meltemi to ease
Leave at noon to cross faster
Motor directly into it
optionExplanations: Above sensible limits for this crew.
Correct: Meltemi spells end; waiting costs only time.
The strongest part of the day.
Head seas and wind beyond limits.
steps.explanation: Stay put when the forecast exceeds your crew's limits.

questions.prompt: A motor cruiser (cruising at 18 knots) and a sailing yacht (6 knots) plan the same 36-mile passage in a 4-hour window before a front. Which statement is right?
options: Both have plenty of time
The motor cruiser fits the window only if it can keep its speed in the expected sea
The yacht is safer because it is slower
Neither should consider speed
optionExplanations: The yacht needs about 6 hours: it does not fit.
Correct: head seas can halve a planing boat's speed.
Slower means longer exposure.
Realistic speed is central to the decision.
questions.explanation: Plan on realistic speed in the expected sea; the yacht does not fit this window at all.
